children.topic: 1. What accounting is and why it matters
children.note: Start here. Accounting is how a business records and reports its money story so owners, lenders, KRA and others can make good decisions. This map covers the basic ideas, users, rules and the road to CPA.

Everything a business owns was paid for either by someone it owes or by its owner. So Assets = Liabilities + Equity, and this must balance after every single transaction. It is the base of double entry and of the statement of financial position.

Double entry records every transaction twice, as a debit in one account and an equal credit in another. Learn what the two sides mean, the DEAD CLIC rules, T-accounts, and how it all proves itself in a trial balance.

children.topic: 4. Source documents and books of prime entry
children.note: Every transaction starts life as a piece of paper or a message. Source documents are the evidence; books of prime entry are where that evidence is first listed in order, before totals are posted to the ledger.

Once transactions are written in the books of prime entry, they are posted to ledger accounts, each account is balanced off, and the balances are listed in a trial balance. A trial balance that agrees is a useful arithmetic check, and it is the starting point for the income statement and the statement of financial position.

children.topic: 6. Final accounts of a sole trader
children.note: At the year end, the trial balance is turned into two reports: a statement of profit or loss (did the business make money?) and a statement of financial position (what it owns and owes). This map shows how, with a full Nairobi shop example.

Some bills are paid late and some are paid early, so the cash paid in a year is rarely the true cost of that year. Accruals and prepayments are year-end adjustments that move income and expenses into the year they belong to, so profit and the statement of financial position are correct.

Big assets such as vehicles and machines are used for many years, so their cost is spread over those years as depreciation. This map covers the key figures, the straight-line and reducing-balance methods, part-year charges, the journal entries and disposals, with worked examples in KES.

children.topic: 9. Bad debts and allowance for receivables
children.note: Some credit customers never pay. This map shows how to write off bad debts, set an allowance for doubtful ones, and show receivables at a realistic amount.

Your cash book and the bank statement both track the same money, but they rarely show the same balance on the same day. A bank reconciliation explains the gap, fixes mistakes in your own books, and proves the bank figure is right. The same idea works for a business M-Pesa Till or Paybill statement.

nodeData.topic: What accounting is and why it matters
nodeData.note: Start here. Accounting is how a business records and reports its money story so owners, lenders, KRA and others can make good decisions. This map covers the basic ideas, users, rules and the road to CPA.

children.note: Accounting is the language of business. It turns everyday money events into clear reports people can trust and use.
Accounting is recording, classifying, summarising and reporting money transactions so that people can make good economic decisions.

manas.q: What is accounting?

children.note: Record → classify → summarise → report. Every topic in this library fits one of these four steps.

manas.q: What are the four steps of the accounting process?

children.note: Writing each transaction down when it happens, with its date, amount and evidence such as a receipt, invoice or M-Pesa message.
Grouping similar items together, for example all sales in one account and all rent payments in another.
Totalling the accounts at the end of a period, usually in a trial balance, so the big picture can be seen.
Presenting the results as financial statements: profit or loss, financial position and cash flows, with notes.
Bookkeeping is the recording part: entering daily transactions in books or software. Accounting goes further: it checks, adjusts, summarises, reports and explains what the numbers mean.

manas.q: How does bookkeeping differ from accounting?

children.note: Records sales, purchases, receipts and payments, keeps ledgers up to date and reconciles M-Pesa and bank statements.
Makes year-end adjustments, prepares financial statements, advises on tax and decisions, and interprets results for owners.
Without records an owner cannot tell if the business makes a profit, how much it owes, or how much tax is due. Lenders and KRA also expect proper books.
An event that changes the money position of a business and can be measured in money, such as a sale, a purchase or paying wages.

manas.q: What is a business transaction?

children.note: Many groups rely on accounts, and each asks a different question. Exam questions often ask you to name users and their needs.
Internal users (owners who run the business, managers) see detailed reports. External users (lenders, KRA, investors, public) mostly see published statements.

manas.q: What is the difference between internal and external users?

children.note: Want to know whether the business makes a profit and whether their capital is safe and growing.
Need detailed costs, budgets and performance figures to plan, control and decide, for example which product to stock.
Want to know if the business can repay loans and interest on time, so they study profits, cash flow and security.
Uses accounts to assess income tax, VAT and other taxes, and to check that declared figures are correct.
Want to judge risk and return: profits, dividends and future prospects before buying or holding shares.
Want to know if jobs are secure and whether the business can afford pay rises and pension contributions.
Suppliers check if they will be paid for goods sold on credit; customers check that a key supplier will survive.
Care about jobs, the environment and local impact, especially for big firms and public bodies.
Accounting has several specialist fields. Each serves different users and leads to different careers.
Prepares general-purpose financial statements for external users, following standards such as IFRS.

manas.q: What is financial accounting?

children.note: Produces internal information: product costs, budgets, variances and decision reports for managers. Not bound by IFRS.

manas.q: What is management accounting?

children.note: Works out taxable income and taxes owed under the law, files returns on KRA's iTax and plans tax legally.
An independent check of financial statements, giving an opinion on whether they give a true and fair view.

manas.q: What is an audit?

children.note: Accounting for government ministries, counties and state bodies, focused on budgets and public money; it uses IPSAS.
Investigates fraud and financial disputes and prepares evidence that can be used in court.
These ground rules guide how every transaction is recorded. Learn each with an example; exams test them often.
The business is treated as separate from its owner. Only business transactions go in its books.

manas.q: What is the business entity concept?

children.note: Achieng owns a duka. Her family's food from the market is not a shop expense; if she takes shop stock home it is drawings.
Only items that can be measured in money are recorded. Staff morale or a good location is not recorded.

manas.q: What is the money measurement concept?

children.note: Accounts assume the business will continue operating for the foreseeable future, so assets are not valued at forced-sale prices.

manas.q: What is the going concern concept?

children.note: A matatu company expects to keep running, so its vehicles are shown at cost less depreciation, not at a quick auction price.
Income and expenses are recorded in the period they are earned or incurred, not when cash moves.

manas.q: What is the accruals concept?

children.note: December electricity used by a pharmacy but paid in January is still a December expense.
Use the same accounting methods from year to year so results can be compared. Change only for a good reason and disclose it.

manas.q: What is the consistency concept?

children.note: Take care under uncertainty: do not overstate assets or income, nor understate liabilities or expenses.

manas.q: What is the prudence concept?

children.note: A customer who owes KES 20,000 has vanished; the debt is written off now rather than hoping to collect.
An item is material if leaving it out or misstating it could change users' decisions. Small items may be treated simply.

manas.q: What is materiality?

children.note: A KES 800 stapler lasts years but is so small it is simply expensed, not depreciated.
Assets are recorded at what they cost when bought, which can be proved with an invoice.

manas.q: What is the historical cost concept?

children.note: Every transaction has two equal effects. This is the basis of double entry and the accounting equation.

manas.q: What is the duality concept?

children.note: Assets = Capital + Liabilities. Duality keeps this equation in balance after every transaction.

manas.q: State the accounting equation.

children.note: The IASB Conceptual Framework says what makes financial information useful. There are two fundamental and four enhancing qualities.
Relevance and faithful representation. Information must have both to be useful.

manas.q: What are the two fundamental qualitative characteristics?

children.note: Information can make a difference to decisions because it helps predict the future or confirm the past. Materiality is part of relevance.
Shows the real economic substance: complete, neutral and free from error.
Comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability make useful information even better.

manas.q: Name the four enhancing qualitative characteristics.

children.note: Users can compare with past years and with other businesses.
Different independent people could agree the figure is fairly shown, for example by checking invoices.
Information reaches users in time to affect their decisions; last year's figures arriving late lose value.
Information is clear and concise for a user with reasonable business knowledge who studies it with care.

children.topic: Who sets the rules in Kenya
children.note: Several bodies shape accounting in Kenya: one examines, one regulates accountants, and standards come from international boards.
The state examinations board that sets and runs professional exams in Kenya, including CPA.

manas.q: What does KASNEB do?

children.note: The Institute of Certified Public Accountants of Kenya, set up under the Accountants Act 2008. It registers, licenses and regulates accountants.

manas.q: What is ICPAK's role?

children.note: Kenya uses IFRS, issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB), for general-purpose financial statements.
A simpler version of IFRS for smaller entities with no public accountability, such as many family businesses.

manas.q: What is IFRS for SMEs?

children.note: Government bodies use International Public Sector Accounting Standards, adapted for Kenya by the Public Sector Accounting Standards Board.
Kenya Revenue Authority collects taxes. It is not a standard setter, but tax law affects what records businesses must keep.
Short examples showing the concepts in action. Check that every debit equals its credit.

children.topic: Then she buys stock for cash

Paying the owner's personal bills from the business is drawings, not an expense. This is the entity concept.
A business can make a profit and still run out of cash, because of credit sales and stock. Accruals explains why.
Bookkeeping is only the recording part. Exams expect you to show the wider role of accounting.
For each user, state what they want to know. A list of names alone scores low marks.
Prudence means caution, not deliberately understating profits or creating secret reserves.
Try each question before opening the answer steps.
Write a definition, then show how bookkeeping is part of accounting.
Accounting records, classifies, summarises and reports financial transactions to help users decide.
Bookkeeping is the routine recording; accounting adds adjusting, reporting and interpreting.

children.topic: Q2: Owner pays home KPLC bill
children.note: Mutua pays his home electricity bill of KES 6,000 from the business bank account. Name the concept and the entry.
Business entity: the bill is personal, not a business cost.
Dr Drawings 6,000 / Cr Bank 6,000.

children.topic: Q3: Prepaid insurance for a matatu
children.note: Kamau pays KES 120,000 on 1 October for 12 months' insurance. Year end is 31 December. What is this year's expense?
October to December = 3 months. Expense = 120,000 × 3/12 = KES 30,000.
Accruals: expense follows the period that benefits, not the payment date.
Name three users of accounts and explain what each needs.
Bank: ability to repay loans. KRA: correct taxable profit. Employees: job security and pay. Any three with needs earn full marks.

children.note: Double entry, the ledger, trial balance and simple financial statements for a learner starting from zero.
Practical skills: iTax, eTIMS, payroll, Excel, accounting software and month-end closing.
Bookkeeper, accounts assistant, accountant, auditor, tax consultant, management accountant, finance manager, CFO, forensic investigator.

nodeData.note: Everything a business owns was paid for either by someone it owes or by its owner. So Assets = Liabilities + Equity, and this must balance after every single transaction. It is the base of double entry and of the statement of financial position.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: The equation is a simple check that the books are complete: both sides must always show the same total.
What the business controls (assets) equals what it owes outsiders (liabilities) plus what belongs to the owner (equity, also called capital).

manas.q: State the basic accounting equation.

children.topic: Two views of the same money
children.note: The left side shows where the money is now (cash, stock, a fridge). The right side shows where it came from (a lender, a supplier, the owner).
The duka is treated as separate from Wanjiku herself. That is why money she puts in is owed back to her as capital.

manas.q: What is the business entity concept?

children.note: Equity is what would be left for the owner if all assets were turned into cash and every debt paid. It is also called net assets.

manas.q: How do you find equity from assets and liabilities?

children.note: Every transaction touches at least two items, so the equation can never go out of balance. Debits and credits are just a way of recording those two sides.
An asset is a resource the business controls because of something in the past, which is expected to bring it future benefit.
A resource controlled by the business, arising from a past event, that should bring economic benefit later, such as cash in, or goods to sell.

manas.q: What is an asset?

children.note: Assets expected to be turned into cash or used up within 12 months, or held mainly for trading. Examples: cash, M-Pesa float, inventory, receivables.

manas.q: What is a current asset?

children.note: Assets kept for use over more than one year, not for resale. Examples: a shop fridge, a matatu, land, computers.

manas.q: What is a non-current asset?

children.note: Amounts customers owe the business for goods sold on credit. They are a current asset because they should be collected soon.
Goods bought to resell, like sugar, flour and soap in a duka. Under IAS 2 Inventories they are measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
A liability is a present duty to give up resources, usually cash, because of something that already happened.
A present obligation of the business, arising from a past event, that it expects to settle by paying out cash or other resources.

manas.q: What is a liability?

children.note: Debts due within 12 months, such as trade payables to suppliers, an overdraft, or unpaid wages and tax.

manas.q: What is a current liability?

children.note: Debts due after more than 12 months, such as a three-year bank loan or a long-term SACCO loan.

manas.q: What is a non-current liability?

children.note: Amounts the business owes suppliers for goods or services bought on credit. A classic current liability.
Equity is the owner's share of the business. For a sole trader it is usually called capital and moves with profits and drawings.
Cash or other assets the owner puts into the business. It increases both assets and capital.

manas.q: What is capital?

children.note: Profit is income minus expenses. It belongs to the owner, so it is added to capital. A loss reduces capital.

manas.q: How does profit affect capital?

children.note: Cash, stock or other assets the owner takes for personal use. They reduce capital directly and are not a business expense.

manas.q: What are drawings?

children.note: Closing capital = Opening capital + Capital introduced + Profit − Drawings. Use it to check the equity section of any balance sheet.

manas.q: What is the closing capital formula?

children.note: Income (sales, fees, commission) raises equity. Expenses (rent, wages, electricity, cost of goods sold) lower equity.
Breaking equity into its parts shows exactly how trading changes the owner's claim.
Assets = Liabilities + Capital + Income − Expenses − Drawings. It is the basic equation with equity split into its moving parts.

manas.q: Write the expanded accounting equation.

children.topic: Why income sits on the right
children.note: Income increases what belongs to the owner, so it sits with capital. When a sale brings in cash, assets rise and income rises by the same amount.

children.topic: Why expenses and drawings are minus
children.note: Both reduce the owner's claim. Expenses are used up in earning income; drawings are simply taken out by the owner.
If the owner adds no capital and takes nothing, the rise in net assets over a period is the profit. Adjust for any capital added and drawings taken.

manas.q: How can profit be found from changes in net assets?

children.note: Every transaction falls into one of a few patterns. Learn the patterns and you can analyse anything.
Example: taking a bank loan. Cash (asset) rises and Loan (liability) rises by the same amount.

manas.q: Give a transaction that increases both sides.

children.note: Example: paying a supplier. Cash falls and Payables fall by the same amount.

manas.q: Give a transaction that decreases both sides.

children.note: Example: buying a fridge for cash. One asset rises, another falls, and the total does not change.

manas.q: What is an asset swap?

children.note: Example: a lender agrees to turn a loan into owner's capital. The right side changes in mix but not in total. Rare at beginner level.
A sale at a profit raises assets and equity; paying rent lowers assets and equity. The equity change is the profit or loss part.
Wanjiku opens a small duka in Kawangware, Nairobi. We record ten transactions and check that Assets = Liabilities + Equity after each one. Figures in KES.
Inventory +80,000; Payables +80,000. Dr Inventory / Cr Payables 80,000. Equation: 280,000 = 80,000 + 200,000.
Stock costing 30,000 sold for 50,000 cash. Cash +50,000, Inventory −30,000, so assets +20,000 and profit +20,000. Equation: 300,000 = 80,000 + 220,000.
Cash −15,000; rent expense reduces equity by 15,000. Dr Rent / Cr Cash 15,000. Equation: 285,000 = 80,000 + 205,000.
Wanjiku sends 10,000 to her personal M-Pesa for school fees. Cash −10,000; Drawings reduce equity. Dr Drawings / Cr Cash. Equation: 275,000 = 80,000 + 195,000.
Cash −50,000; Payables −50,000. Dr Payables / Cr Cash 50,000. Equation: 225,000 = 30,000 + 195,000.
Paid in cash. Equipment +60,000; Cash −60,000. An asset swap. Dr Equipment / Cr Cash. Equation stays 225,000 = 30,000 + 195,000.
A three-year loan paid into the account. Cash +100,000; Loan +100,000. Dr Cash / Cr Loan. Equation: 325,000 = 130,000 + 195,000.

children.topic: T9: Credit sale to a hotel
children.note: Stock costing 20,000 sold for 32,000 on credit. Receivables +32,000, Inventory −20,000, profit +12,000. Equation: 337,000 = 130,000 + 207,000.
Cash +20,000; Receivables −20,000. Dr Cash / Cr Receivables. An asset swap, so the equation stays 337,000 = 130,000 + 207,000.
Cash 235,000 + Inventory 30,000 + Receivables 12,000 + Fridge 60,000 = 337,000. Payables 30,000 + Loan 100,000 = 130,000. Equity 207,000.
Liabilities 130,000 + Capital 200,000 + Income 82,000 − Expenses 65,000 (cost of sales 50,000, rent 15,000) − Drawings 10,000 = 337,000. It matches assets.
Sales 82,000 − Cost of sales 50,000 = Gross profit 32,000. Less rent 15,000 = Net profit 17,000. Capital: 200,000 + 17,000 − 10,000 = 207,000.
The equation laid out as a report: Wanjiku's Duka at the end of the period. Depreciation on the fridge is ignored to keep it simple.
A snapshot of assets, liabilities and equity on one date. It is the accounting equation in report form, also called a balance sheet.

manas.q: What is a statement of financial position?

children.note: Fridge (equipment) 60,000. In real books it would be shown after depreciation under IAS 16, or Section 17 of IFRS for SMEs.
Inventory 30,000 + Receivables 12,000 + Cash at bank 235,000 = 277,000. Total assets = 60,000 + 277,000 = 337,000.
Capital introduced 200,000, add net profit 17,000, less drawings 10,000 = 207,000.
Non-current: bank loan 100,000. Current: trade payables 30,000. Any loan instalment due within 12 months would move to current liabilities.
Capital 207,000 + Liabilities 130,000 = 337,000, equal to total assets. The statement balances.
Most errors come from putting an item on the wrong side or in the wrong category.
Wrong. Drawings are the owner taking value out; they reduce capital, not profit. Wanjiku's 10,000 does not appear in the income statement.

manas.q: Are drawings an expense?

children.note: Wrong. A loan must be repaid, so it is a liability. It raises cash and liabilities but leaves profit untouched.

manas.q: Is a bank loan income?

children.topic: Full sale price added to profit
children.note: Only sales minus cost of the goods sold is profit. In T3, profit is 20,000, not 50,000.

children.topic: Owner's money mixed with the shop's
children.note: Personal spending paid from the till must be recorded as drawings. Keep separate M-Pesa tills or accounts if possible.
Buying on credit does not reduce cash. It increases inventory and payables until the supplier is paid.
Classify by when the item is due or used up: within 12 months is current. Stock is current even if some lasts longer.

maps.title: CA11 · 3. Double entry: debits and credits

nodeData.note: Double entry records every transaction twice, as a debit in one account and an equal credit in another. Learn what the two sides mean, the DEAD CLIC rules, T-accounts, and how it all proves itself in a trial balance.

children.note: Double entry rests on one idea: each business event changes at least two things, so it is written in at least two accounts. That is how the books stay balanced.
Every transaction gives something and receives something of equal value. One account receives value (debit) and another gives it (credit), for the same amount.

manas.q: What is the dual aspect concept?

children.topic: Total debits always equal total credits
children.note: For every transaction the debit amounts add up to the credit amounts. One entry may have several debits or credits, but the two totals must match.

manas.q: What must be true of every double-entry transaction?

children.note: An account is a separate record for one item, such as Cash, Sales, Rent or a named customer. The full set of accounts is called the ledger.

manas.q: What is a ledger account?

children.note: Assets = Liabilities + Capital. Each entry changes the equation by equal amounts on both sides, or swaps value within one side, so it always holds.

manas.q: State the accounting equation.

children.note: Write it as Assets + Expenses + Drawings = Liabilities + Capital + Income. The left side holds the debit-balance items; the right side holds the credit-balance items.

manas.q: What is the expanded accounting equation?

children.note: Two-sided recording lets you prove the arithmetic with a trial balance, find many errors, and build the income statement and balance sheet straight from the accounts.
The method grew among Italian merchants. Luca Pacioli described it in print in Venice in 1494, and it is still the basis of every accounting system and package today.

children.topic: Worked example: stock bought for cash
children.note: A duka buys stock for KES 50,000 cash. Dr Purchases KES 50,000 / Cr Cash KES 50,000. Debits 50,000 = credits 50,000.

children.topic: Debit and credit mean left and right
children.note: Debit and credit are just positions in an account: debit is the left side, credit is the right side. They are not good news or bad news.
A debit is any amount written on the left-hand side of an account. Short form: Dr.

manas.q: Which side of an account is the debit side?

children.note: A credit is any amount written on the right-hand side of an account. Short form: Cr.

manas.q: Which side of an account is the credit side?

children.note: A credit is not automatically a gain and a debit is not a loss. Whether a debit increases or decreases an account depends on the type of account.
Your deposit is a liability for the bank (it owes you), so the bank credits your account. In your own books the same money is an asset and is debited.

children.topic: Where Dr and Cr come from
children.note: The short forms come from Latin words linked to owing and trusting: debere and credere. Learn them as labels for left and right.
Each kind of account has a side that increases it. The memory aid DEAD CLIC tells you which side, and the opposite side always decreases it.
Debit increases Expenses, Assets and Drawings. DEAD = Debit, Expenses, Assets, Drawings.

manas.q: What does DEAD stand for in DEAD CLIC?

children.note: Credit increases Liabilities, Income and Capital. CLIC = Credit, Liabilities, Income, Capital.

manas.q: What does CLIC stand for in DEAD CLIC?

children.note: Things the business owns or controls, such as cash, bank, stock, equipment and money owed by customers. Increase with a debit, decrease with a credit.
Costs of running the business, such as rent, salaries and electricity. Increase with a debit.
Cash or goods the owner takes for personal use. Drawings reduce capital, so they are debited, but they are NOT a business expense.

manas.q: Which side increases drawings, and are drawings an expense?

children.note: Amounts the business owes, such as suppliers, a SACCO loan or KRA. Increase with a credit, decrease with a debit.
What the owner has invested in the business, plus profits kept. Increases with a credit.
Sales and other earnings such as discount received or rent received. Increase with a credit.
To reduce any account, post to the side opposite its increase side. Paying cash out is a credit to Cash; paying a supplier is a debit to that supplier.

manas.q: How do you record a decrease in an account?

children.note: The side an account usually ends on: debit for assets, expenses and drawings; credit for liabilities, capital and income.

manas.q: What is the normal balance of a liability account?

children.note: A T-account is a simple sketch of a ledger account shaped like the letter T: name on top, debits on the left, credits on the right.
Write the account name across the top bar. Debits go under the left arm, credits under the right arm, each with date, other account name and amount.

manas.q: What is a T-account?

children.note: In each line, write the name of the account that holds the other half of the entry. This lets you trace every posting both ways.
Add both sides. Put the difference on the smaller side as 'balance c/d' so both totals match, then bring it down on the other side as 'balance b/d'.

manas.q: How do you balance a T-account?

children.note: If debits exceed credits the account has a debit balance (usually an asset, expense or drawings). If credits are bigger, it has a credit balance.
List every closing balance in a debit or credit column. If double entry was done correctly, the two column totals agree.

manas.q: What is a trial balance?

children.note: Juma opens a small shop in Nairobi in October 2026. Follow 13 entries, then the T-accounts, trial balance and equation check. Bank includes M-Pesa till money.
Each bubble below gives one journal entry as Dr / Cr with KES amounts. In every one, debits equal credits.
Juma puts KES 200,000 into the business bank account. Dr Bank 200,000 / Cr Capital 200,000. Asset up, capital up.
A SACCO lends KES 100,000, paid into bank. Dr Bank 100,000 / Cr Loan (SACCO) 100,000. Asset up, liability up.
Shop shelves cost KES 20,000, paid from bank. Dr Fixtures and fittings 20,000 / Cr Bank 20,000. One asset up, another down.
Goods for resale KES 80,000 on credit from Mombasa Wholesalers. Dr Purchases 80,000 / Cr Mombasa Wholesalers (payable) 80,000.
Goods sold for KES 30,000 cash. Dr Cash 30,000 / Cr Sales 30,000. Asset up, income up.
Goods sold on credit to Wanjiru for KES 25,000. Dr Wanjiru (receivable) 25,000 / Cr Sales 25,000.
Wanjiru returns goods worth KES 3,000. Dr Returns inwards 3,000 / Cr Wanjiru 3,000. She now owes 22,000.
Juma returns faulty goods of KES 5,000 to Mombasa Wholesalers. Dr Mombasa Wholesalers 5,000 / Cr Returns outwards 5,000. He now owes 75,000.
Wanjiru settles her KES 22,000 by M-Pesa paying 21,000; Juma allows 1,000 discount. Dr Bank 21,000, Dr Discount allowed 1,000 / Cr Wanjiru 22,000.
Juma clears the KES 75,000 owed, paying 73,000 by bank after a 2,000 discount. Dr Mombasa Wholesalers 75,000 / Cr Bank 73,000, Cr Discount received 2,000.
Shop rent of KES 15,000 paid by bank. Dr Rent 15,000 / Cr Bank 15,000. Expense up, asset down.
Shop assistant paid KES 12,000 in cash. Dr Salaries 12,000 / Cr Cash 12,000.
Juma takes KES 4,000 cash for family use. Dr Drawings 4,000 / Cr Cash 4,000. Not an expense of the shop.
Posting all 13 entries gives the balances below. Each bubble shows how the account was balanced off.
Dr side: 30,000. Cr side: 12,000 + 4,000 = 16,000. Balance c/d 14,000 (debit balance).
Dr: 25,000. Cr: 3,000 + 22,000 = 25,000. Both sides total 25,000, so the balance is nil: she has paid in full.
Cr: 80,000. Dr: 5,000 + 75,000 = 80,000. Nil balance: the supplier is fully paid.

Debit balances: Fixtures 20,000; Purchases 80,000; Returns inwards 3,000; Discount allowed 1,000; Rent 15,000; Salaries 12,000; Drawings 4,000. Credit: Capital 200,000; Loan 100,000; Returns outwards 5,000; Discount received 2,000.
Proof that the books balance, built from the T-account balances.

Capital 200,000 + Loan 100,000 + Sales 55,000 + Returns out 5,000 + Discount received 2,000 = 362,000. Matches the debit column.
Assets 247,000 (bank 213,000, cash 14,000, fixtures 20,000) + expenses 111,000 + drawings 4,000 = 362,000. Liabilities 100,000 + capital 200,000 + income 62,000 = 362,000.
Most beginner errors come from reversing a side or using the wrong account. Some errors still leave the trial balance agreeing.
Students credit cash when money comes in because 'credit' sounds positive. Money in is always Dr Cash or Dr Bank.
Drawings reduce capital, not profit. Never put them in the income statement.
Returns inwards are sales returns (goods coming back from customers): debit. Returns outwards are purchase returns (goods sent back to suppliers): credit.

manas.q: What are returns inwards and returns outwards?

children.note: Trade discount is deducted on the invoice before any entry, so it is never posted. Only cash or settlement discounts have their own accounts.

manas.q: Is trade discount recorded in the ledger?

children.note: Discount allowed is given to customers: an expense, debit. Discount received is from suppliers: income, credit. Under IFRS 15, an expected settlement discount reduces revenue instead.

manas.q: Which side are discount allowed and discount received?

children.note: If Juma takes stock costing KES 6,000 for home: Dr Drawings 6,000 / Cr Purchases 6,000. Do not credit Sales.
Omission, commission, principle, original entry, complete reversal and compensating errors all leave totals equal, so an agreeing trial balance is not proof of accuracy.

manas.q: Name six errors that do not affect trial balance agreement.

children.note: Posting to the wrong class of account, such as debiting a new van to Motor expenses instead of the Motor vehicles asset account.
Correct accounts and amount, but debit and credit swapped. Example: a cash sale posted Dr Sales / Cr Cash. Totals still agree.
Try each one, then open its bubbles for the answer steps.
A matatu owner buys a vehicle for KES 1,500,000 on credit from a dealer. Give the entry.
Motor vehicles is an asset that increases. The dealer is a liability (payable) that increases.
Asset up = debit; liability up = credit. Dr Motor vehicles 1,500,000 / Cr Payable (dealer) 1,500,000.
Cash Dr: 50,000 and 18,000. Cash Cr: 22,000, 9,500 and 6,000. Find the balance.
Balance c/d 30,500 on the credit side so both sides total 68,000; bring down 30,500 as a debit balance b/d.
Rent of KES 8,000 paid by bank was posted Dr Bank / Cr Rent. What error is this, and what is the correction?
Right accounts and amount, sides swapped: an error of complete reversal. The trial balance still agrees.
Post double the amount the right way: Dr Rent 16,000 / Cr Bank 16,000. This cancels the wrong entry and records the right one.
A customer owing KES 40,000 pays KES 38,000 by M-Pesa in full settlement. Give the entry.
38,000 arrives in the bank; the 2,000 shortfall is discount allowed.
Dr Bank 38,000, Dr Discount allowed 2,000 / Cr Receivable 40,000. Debits 40,000 = credits 40,000.

maps.title: CA11 · 4. Source documents and books of prime entry

nodeData.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
nodeData.note: Every transaction starts life as a piece of paper or a message. Source documents are the evidence; books of prime entry are where that evidence is first listed in order, before totals are posted to the ledger.

children.note: Before anything reaches the ledger it must be backed by evidence and listed in one place. This keeps the ledger short and makes errors easy to trace.
The original record that proves a transaction happened, such as an invoice, receipt or M-Pesa message. Nothing should be recorded without one.

manas.q: What is a source document?

children.topic: What is a book of prime entry?
children.note: A book (or software screen) where transactions are first written down in date order, grouped by type, before posting to the ledger. Also called a book of original entry or day book.

manas.q: What is a book of prime entry?

children.note: Source document → book of prime entry → ledger accounts → trial balance → financial statements. Each step summarises the one before it.

children.topic: Why not post straight to the ledger?
children.note: Posting totals instead of hundreds of single items saves time, cuts errors and gives an audit trail from the ledger back to each document.
The common documents a Kenyan business meets every day, and which book each one feeds.
Written by the buyer to ask a supplier for goods at agreed prices. It records no accounting entry but is the start of an authorised purchase.

manas.q: Does a purchase order create an accounting entry?

children.note: Comes with the goods and is signed by the buyer as proof of receipt. It is matched to the order and invoice; it creates no entry by itself.
Sent by the seller showing goods, prices, discounts and amount due on credit. Seller records it in the sales day book; buyer in the purchases day book.

manas.q: Which day books does an invoice feed for seller and buyer?

children.note: Issued by a seller to reduce what a customer owes, for example after goods are returned or overcharged. Seller: sales returns day book; buyer: purchases returns day book.

manas.q: What is a credit note and who issues it?

children.note: Sent by a buyer to a supplier asking for a credit, e.g. for faulty goods returned. It supports the purchases returns entry until the supplier's credit note arrives.

manas.q: What is a debit note?

children.note: Written proof that money was received. The business keeps a copy of receipts it issues, which supports entries on the debit side of the cash book.
The stub left in the cheque book after a cheque is written. It shows date, payee and amount and supports a bank payment in the cash book.
An internal form showing what is being paid, to whom and why, signed by the person approving it. Common in Kenyan offices, hospitals and SACCOs.
The bank's record of the account. It shows charges, interest, standing orders and direct credits the business may not yet know about, and is used for bank reconciliation.
The confirmation SMS and the till or paybill statement are evidence of mobile-money receipts and payments. Treat the M-Pesa account like a bank column in the cash book.

eTIMS is KRA's electronic Tax Invoice Management System. Invoices are generated through it and sent to KRA, and buyers generally need valid eTIMS invoices to support expense and VAT claims (check current KRA guidance).

manas.q: What is eTIMS?

children.note: Before paying a supplier, check that the order, goods received and invoice agree on items, quantities and prices. This three-way match stops paying for goods never received.

children.topic: The day books for credit trade
children.note: Credit sales, credit purchases and returns each get their own list. Only credit items go here; cash items go to the cash book.
Lists credit sales invoices issued, in date order: date, customer, invoice number, amount. Its total is posted to sales.

manas.q: What does the sales day book record?

children.note: Lists credit purchase invoices received for goods bought for resale (or materials). Its total is posted to purchases.

manas.q: What does the purchases day book record?

children.note: Also called returns inwards day book. Lists credit notes issued to customers for goods they sent back.

manas.q: What is another name for the sales returns day book?

children.note: Also called returns outwards day book. Lists goods returned to suppliers, supported by debit notes sent and credit notes received.
Day books often have extra columns, such as VAT or product lines, so each total can go to the right account. Use the VAT rate on the tax invoice (check the current KRA rate).
The cash book is both a book of prime entry and a ledger account for cash and bank. Receipts go on the left (debit), payments on the right (credit).
Has a cash column and a bank column on each side. Cash and bank balances are worked out separately.

manas.q: What columns does a two-column cash book have?

children.note: Adds a discount column on each side: discount allowed on the receipts side, discount received on the payments side.

manas.q: Which discount goes on which side of a three-column cash book?

children.note: The discount columns are not part of the cash or bank balance. They are just totalled and posted to the ledger.

manas.q: Are the discount columns balanced like cash and bank?

children.note: Moving money between cash and bank, such as banking takings, appears on both sides and is marked 'C'. No other ledger posting is needed.

manas.q: What is a contra entry in the cash book?

children.note: If payments exceed receipts in the bank column, the balance b/d is on the credit side. That means the bank is owed money.
Many Kenyan businesses add an M-Pesa column, or keep one per bank account. The rules are the same as for the bank column.

children.topic: Petty cash and the imprest system
children.note: Small office payments such as matatu fare, tea or photocopying are paid from a petty cash box kept by a petty cashier.
A fixed float is set. At the end of the period the cashier is given exactly what was spent, so the float goes back to the same amount.

manas.q: How does the imprest system work?

children.note: Each payment is supported by a signed voucher, with a receipt attached where possible. Vouchers are numbered in order.
Receipts on the left, payments on the right split into columns like travel, stationery and refreshments. Column totals are posted to expense accounts.
Amount to restore the float = imprest − cash in hand = total of vouchers. Any difference means cash is missing or a voucher is lost.

manas.q: How do you calculate the petty cash reimbursement?

children.note: The journal is for anything that does not fit the other books. Each entry shows the debit, the credit and a short narration.
Date; account debited and amount; account credited and amount (indented); then a narration explaining why.

manas.q: What are the parts of a journal entry?

children.note: Record a business's assets, liabilities and capital when books are first opened. Capital is the balancing figure.
Errors found later, like posting to the wrong account, are fixed by a journal, not by crossing out the ledger.
A van or fridge bought on credit is not stock for resale, so it goes in the journal, not the purchases day book.

manas.q: Where do you record a non-current asset bought on credit?

children.note: Year-end adjustments, depreciation, bad debts written off, drawings of goods and transfers between accounts all go through the journal.
Individual items go to personal accounts; the period totals go to the impersonal (nominal) accounts.
Each invoice: debit the customer's personal account. Total: Dr Trade receivables (control) / Cr Sales.

manas.q: What is the double entry for the sales day book total?

children.note: Each invoice: credit the supplier's account. Total: Dr Purchases / Cr Trade payables (control).
Sales returns: Dr Sales returns / Cr Trade receivables. Purchases returns: Dr Trade payables / Cr Purchases returns.
Discount allowed total: Dr Discount allowed / Cr Trade receivables. Discount received total: Dr Trade payables / Cr Discount received.

manas.q: How are the discount column totals posted?

children.note: A reference column showing where each item was posted, such as SL12 or GL4. It proves posting is done and helps tracing.
Small, complete examples that add up. Work them with a pencil before reading the answers.
March: credit sales to Kamau 20,000, Otieno 10,000 and Achieng 15,000 = 45,000. Credit purchases from Bidco 30,000 and Mombasa Supplies 12,000 = 42,000.
Dr Trade receivables 45,000 / Cr Sales 45,000. Dr Purchases 42,000 / Cr Trade payables 42,000. Each customer and supplier account is also updated item by item.
Achieng returns goods worth 3,000: Dr Sales returns 3,000 / Cr Trade receivables 3,000. Wanjiku returns 2,000 to Mombasa Supplies: Dr Trade payables 2,000 / Cr Purchases returns 2,000.

1 Mar balances: cash 8,000, bank 45,000. 3: rent by cheque 15,000. 5: cash sales 12,000. 8: Kamau pays 20,000 debt by cheque, less 600 discount. 10: pays Bidco 30,000 by bank, 1,000 discount. 12: banks 10,000 cash. 15: Otieno pays 10,000 debt in cash, less 300 discount. 20: wages 6,000 cash.
Dr Discount allowed 900 / Cr Trade receivables 900. Dr Trade payables 1,000 / Cr Discount received 1,000. The contra needs no further posting.

children.topic: Imprest petty cash book of KES 10,000
children.note: 1 Apr: float of 10,000 drawn from bank. Vouchers: matatu fares 1,200, tea and milk 800, stationery 2,500, courier 1,500, cleaning 1,000.
Spent 1,200 + 800 + 2,500 + 1,500 + 1,000 = 7,000. Cash in hand 10,000 − 7,000 = 3,000, which should match a count of the box.
Setting up: Dr Petty cash 10,000 / Cr Bank 10,000. Expenses: Dr Travel 1,200, Refreshments 800, Stationery 2,500, Postage 1,500, Cleaning 1,000 / Cr Petty cash 7,000.
Dr Petty cash 7,000 / Cr Bank 7,000. Balance c/d is back to 10,000, ready for May.
Three typical journal entries for a small hospital pharmacy.
Dr Equipment 150,000, Inventory 60,000, Bank 45,000, Cash 8,000 (total 263,000) / Cr Trade payables 33,000, Capital 230,000 (total 263,000).
Dr Equipment 120,000 / Cr Other payables (Hotpoint) 120,000. Narration: vaccine fridge bought on 60-day credit, invoice no. 4471.
Rent of 5,000 was posted to repairs. Dr Rent 5,000 / Cr Repairs 5,000. Narration: correction of error.
Good paperwork stops fraud and errors before they reach the ledger.
Purchases, payments and credit notes must be approved by a named person within set limits before they are processed.

manas.q: Why must payments be authorised?

children.note: Invoices, credit notes, receipts and vouchers are pre-numbered. Gaps or duplicates show a missing or fake document.

manas.q: Why are source documents pre-numbered?

children.note: Different people should order, receive, record and pay. The petty cashier should not also approve vouchers or reconcile the box.

manas.q: What is segregation of duties?

children.note: Count petty cash without notice and reconcile the cash book with bank and M-Pesa statements every month.
Stamp invoices and vouchers 'PAID' with the date so they cannot be presented for payment twice.
The errors examiners most often see in this topic.

children.topic: Cash sales in the sales day book
children.note: The sales day book is for credit sales only. Cash sales go straight to the cash book.

children.topic: Asset purchases in the purchases day book
children.note: Only goods for resale go in the purchases day book. Equipment and vehicles on credit go in the journal.
Discount allowed (we give) sits with receipts; discount received (we get) sits with payments. Trade discount is never recorded at all.

manas.q: Is trade discount recorded in the books?

children.note: Students carry down a 'balance' on the discount columns. They are only totalled, never balanced.
A cash-to-bank transfer is complete within the cash book. Posting it again to a ledger account doubles it.
Modern standards treat expected settlement discounts as reducing revenue rather than as an expense. At the basics stage, follow the method the question asks for.
Try each one before opening the answer steps.

children.topic: Q1: Supplier credit note — which book?
children.note: A business receives a credit note from a supplier for damaged goods returned.
It is recorded in the purchases returns (returns outwards) day book.
Dr Supplier (trade payables) / Cr Purchases returns.
How much must be given to the petty cashier to restore the imprest?
10,000 − 2,350 = 7,650, which should equal the total of the vouchers.
A customer owing 50,000 pays by cheque, taking a 2% cash discount. Show the cash book entries.
2% × 50,000 = 1,000 in the discount allowed column (receipts side).
50,000 − 1,000 = 49,000 in the bank column (receipts side). Customer's account is credited 50,000 in total.
A delivery van is bought on credit for KES 1,200,000. Name the book and the entry.
General journal: Dr Motor vehicles 1,200,000 / Cr Other payables 1,200,000, with a narration.

maps.title: CA11 · 5. Ledgers and the trial balance

nodeData.note: Once transactions are written in the books of prime entry, they are posted to ledger accounts, each account is balanced off, and the balances are listed in a trial balance. A trial balance that agrees is a useful arithmetic check, and it is the starting point for the income statement and the statement of financial position.

children.topic: What ledgers are and why they matter
children.note: A ledger is the main book where every account lives. Books of prime entry record transactions in date order; ledgers sort them by account so you can see the total for each item.
One page (or one record in software) for a single item such as Rent, Bank or a customer. It has a debit side on the left and a credit side on the right.

manas.q: What is a ledger account?

children.note: Holds the main accounts: assets, liabilities, capital, income and expenses. In many businesses it also holds the receivables and payables control accounts that summarise the subsidiary ledgers.

manas.q: What does the general (nominal) ledger contain?

children.note: A separate ledger with one account for each credit customer, showing what each owes. Example: a pharmacy keeps accounts for each clinic that buys medicines on credit.

manas.q: What is the receivables (sales) ledger?

children.note: A separate ledger with one account for each credit supplier, showing what the business owes each one, for example Kamau Wholesalers or a drug distributor.

manas.q: What is the payables (purchases) ledger?

children.note: Splitting lets different staff work at the same time, keeps the general ledger short, and makes it easy to answer 'how much does this customer owe?' quickly.
Software such as QuickBooks, Sage or Xero still keeps ledgers; it just posts automatically. Knowing the manual method helps you trust and fix what the software shows.

children.topic: Posting from books of prime entry
children.note: Posting means copying entries from the books of prime entry into the ledger accounts, with the date, the name of the other account and the amount.
Sales day book, purchases day book, returns day books, cash book, petty cash book and the journal. Transactions are recorded here first, before any ledger.

manas.q: Name the main books of prime entry.

children.note: Each invoice is debited to that customer's account in the receivables ledger. The period total is credited to Sales in the general ledger (and debited to the receivables control account).
Each supplier invoice is credited to that supplier's account in the payables ledger. The total is debited to Purchases in the general ledger (and credited to the payables control account).

children.topic: Cash book: prime entry and ledger
children.note: The cash book is both a book of prime entry and the ledger account for cash and bank. Only the other side needs posting, for example receipts go to the credit of a customer or Sales.
Used for unusual items: opening entries, buying non-current assets on credit, corrections of errors and year-end adjustments. Each entry shows Dr, Cr and a short narrative.
A column showing where an entry came from or went to, such as SDB 4 or GL 12. It creates an audit trail and shows that an item has already been posted.
At the end of a period each account is totalled and the difference between its two sides is worked out. That difference is the balance carried down to start the next period.

1) Add both sides. 2) Write the difference on the smaller side as 'Balance c/d'. 3) Show equal totals on both sides. 4) Bring the balance down on the opposite side as 'Balance b/d' on the first day of the next period.

manas.q: What are the steps to balance off a ledger account?

children.note: c/d means carried down, written at the end of the period on the smaller side. b/d means brought down, written on the opposite side at the start of the next period.

manas.q: What do 'balance c/d' and 'balance b/d' mean?

children.note: If the debit side is bigger, the account has a debit balance (brought down on the debit side). If the credit side is bigger, it has a credit balance.

manas.q: How do you tell if an account has a debit or credit balance?

children.note: A Nairobi duka's Bank account. Debits: 1 Mar balance b/d 45,000; 5 Mar Sales 30,000; 18 Mar Otieno 12,000 = KES 87,000. Credits: 8 Mar Rent 20,000; 15 Mar Purchases 25,000; 28 Mar Drawings 8,000 = KES 53,000.
Debits 87,000 minus credits 53,000 = KES 34,000. The debit side is larger, so this is a debit balance.
Write 31 Mar Balance c/d 34,000 on the credit side. Both sides now total KES 87,000 and are ruled off.
Write 1 Apr Balance b/d 34,000 on the debit side. The duka starts April with KES 34,000 in the bank, an asset.
Payables ledger account. Credit: 3 Mar Purchases 60,000. Debits: 10 Mar Returns outwards 5,000; 25 Mar Bank 40,000.
Credits 60,000 minus debits 45,000 = KES 15,000. Write Balance c/d 15,000 on the debit side so both sides total 60,000.
Balance b/d 15,000 appears on the credit side on 1 Apr. The business still owes Kamau KES 15,000, a liability.
If an account has only one entry, no balancing is needed; that entry is the balance. Accounts with equal sides are simply ruled off with no balance.
A list of every ledger balance at one date, debit balances in one column and credit balances in another. If double entry was done properly, the two column totals are equal.
A trial balance is a list of all the balances in the ledgers at a particular date, set out in debit and credit columns, to check that total debits equal total credits.

manas.q: What is a trial balance?

children.note: It checks the arithmetic of the double entry, gives a summary of all balances in one place, and is the base for preparing the financial statements.

manas.q: Give three purposes of a trial balance.

children.note: Heading with the business name and 'Trial balance as at [date]'. Columns: account name, Dr (KES), Cr (KES). Totals are double-underlined at the bottom.

manas.q: What is the format of a trial balance?

children.topic: It is not a financial statement
children.note: A trial balance is an internal working list. It is not published and is not the statement of financial position, even though both list balances.
Drawings, Expenses, Assets (including purchases and opening inventory) and Debtors (receivables) normally have debit balances. Memory aid: DEAD CLIC.
Non-current assets, inventory, receivables, bank and cash have debit balances. An overdrawn bank account is the exception: it is a credit balance.

manas.q: Which side do asset balances go on in a trial balance?

children.note: Rent, wages, electricity, carriage, discounts allowed, returns inwards and purchases are debit balances.

manas.q: Is returns inwards a debit or credit balance?

children.note: Money or goods the owner takes for personal use reduce capital, so drawings carry a debit balance.
Capital, Liabilities, Income and Creditors (payables) normally have credit balances.
Trade payables, loans (for example a SACCO or bank loan), accruals and a bank overdraft are credit balances.

manas.q: Which side do liabilities and loans go on in a trial balance?

children.note: What the owner has put into the business, plus retained profits. It is a credit balance because the business owes it to the owner.
Sales, rent received, commission received, discounts received and returns outwards are credit balances.
The trial balance shows opening inventory (from last year). Closing inventory is counted at year end and is usually given as a note below the trial balance, not in it.
Baraka Duka, a general shop in Machakos owned by Mwende. Trial balance as at 31 December 2025, all amounts in KES. 15 accounts; both columns total KES 3,737,000.
Motor vehicle 850,000; Fixtures and fittings 180,000. Subtotal KES 1,030,000 debit.
Inventory at 1 Jan 2025 240,000; Trade receivables 95,000; Bank 132,000; Cash and M-Pesa till 18,000. Subtotal KES 485,000 debit.
Purchases 1,460,000; Rent 240,000; Wages 360,000; Electricity 42,000. Subtotal KES 2,102,000 debit.
Drawings 120,000 debit. Mwende took this for personal and family use during the year.
Capital 899,000; SACCO loan 300,000; Trade payables 128,000; Sales 2,410,000. Total credits KES 3,737,000.

children.topic: Errors the trial balance will not reveal
children.note: Some mistakes keep debits equal to credits, so the trial balance still agrees. Agreement proves the arithmetic, not that the books are correct.
Omission, Original entry, Principle, Reversal, Commission, Compensating. Six errors that leave the trial balance in agreement.

manas.q: Name the six errors not revealed by a trial balance.

children.note: A transaction is left out completely. Example: a KES 8,000 credit sale to Achieng is never entered, so neither Sales nor Achieng's account is touched.

manas.q: What is an error of omission?

children.note: Correct amount, correct type of account, but the wrong person's account. Example: KES 5,000 received from Otieno is credited to Odhiambo's account.

manas.q: What is an error of commission?

children.note: An item is posted to the wrong class of account. Example: a laptop costing KES 70,000 is debited to Office expenses instead of Equipment, an asset.

manas.q: What is an error of principle?

children.note: The wrong amount is entered in the book of prime entry, so both sides use it. Example: an invoice for KES 4,750 is recorded as 4,570 in the day book and posted both ways.

manas.q: What is an error of original entry?

children.note: The right accounts and amount, but debit and credit are swapped. Example: rent paid KES 20,000 is posted Dr Bank / Cr Rent instead of Dr Rent / Cr Bank.

manas.q: What is a complete reversal of entries?

children.note: Two separate mistakes of the same amount cancel out. Example: Sales is overcast by KES 1,000 and Wages is also overcast by KES 1,000.

manas.q: What are compensating errors?

children.topic: Errors the trial balance does reveal
children.note: When only one side is wrong, debits no longer equal credits and the totals differ. These errors must be found and fixed.
Only one side is posted. Example: wages of KES 15,000 are debited to Wages but never credited to Bank.
Both sides are posted on the same side. The difference in the totals is twice the amount.
Example: Dr Purchases 6,300 but Cr Kamau 3,600. A transposition like this gives a difference divisible by 9 (here 2,700).

manas.q: What clue does a difference divisible by 9 give?

children.note: An account is added up wrongly, or its balance is worked out wrongly, so the figure taken to the trial balance is wrong.
A balance is left out of the trial balance, copied wrongly, or put in the wrong column.
If the totals differ, the difference is put into a temporary suspense account so the trial balance agrees while the error is found.
A temporary account holding the difference on a trial balance until the errors are found. It should be cleared to nil before final accounts are finished.

manas.q: What is a suspense account?

children.note: Debits total 3,737,000 and credits 3,728,000, because Sales was balanced as 2,401,000 instead of 2,410,000. Open Suspense with a KES 9,000 credit balance.
Once found, journal: Dr Suspense 9,000 / Cr Sales 9,000. Suspense is now nil and Sales shows the correct 2,410,000. Full treatment comes in the correction of errors map.

children.topic: From trial balance to financial statements
children.note: Each balance goes to one of two statements. Income and expense items build the income statement; assets, liabilities, capital and drawings build the statement of financial position.
Sales, purchases, opening inventory and expenses go to the income statement. Non-current and current assets, liabilities, capital and drawings go to the statement of financial position.

manas.q: Which trial balance items go to the income statement?

children.note: Closing inventory counted at KES 260,000. Cost of sales = 240,000 + 1,460,000 - 260,000 = 1,440,000. Gross profit = 2,410,000 - 1,440,000 = 970,000.
Expenses: rent 240,000 + wages 360,000 + electricity 42,000 = 642,000. Net profit = 970,000 - 642,000 = KES 328,000, before adjustments like depreciation.
Accruals, prepayments, depreciation and allowances for receivables are added after the trial balance, often in an extended trial balance.
These slips cost marks in KASNEB and other exams. Check each one before you hand in.
Balance c/d goes on the smaller side at the end; b/d goes on the other side at the start of the next period. Never both on the same side.

children.topic: Putting closing inventory in the TB
children.note: Only opening inventory is a ledger balance in the trial balance. Closing inventory is an adjustment note.
An overdraft is money owed to the bank, so it is a credit balance, not an asset.
Returns inwards (sales returns) is a debit; returns outwards (purchase returns) is a credit. Students often swap them.
Agreement does not prove accuracy. The six errors of omission, commission, principle, original entry, reversal and compensating all slip through.
A trial balance is 'as at' a date, because it is a snapshot. Marks are lost for writing 'for the year ended'.

maps.title: CA11 · 6. Final accounts of a sole trader

nodeData.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
nodeData.note: At the year end, the trial balance is turned into two reports: a statement of profit or loss (did the business make money?) and a statement of financial position (what it owns and owes). This map shows how, with a full Nairobi shop example.

children.note: At the end of the year the owner wants two answers: did I make money, and what is my business worth? Final accounts answer both, using the balances from the trial balance.
A business owned by one person, like a duka owner or a boda boda operator. The owner keeps all the profit and carries all the risk, even if they employ staff.

manas.q: What is a sole trader?

children.note: The end-of-period reports made from the trial balance: the statement of profit or loss and the statement of financial position.

manas.q: What are the final accounts of a sole trader?

children.note: The time the accounts cover, usually one year, for example 1 January to 31 December. Profit is measured for the period; the financial position is shown on the last day.

manas.q: What is an accounting period?

children.note: The owner, the bank when giving a loan, KRA when checking the tax return, suppliers giving credit, and a buyer if the shop is ever sold.
Even with one owner, the accounts show only the business. Money the owner takes for home use is drawings, not a business expense (business entity concept from topic 1).

children.topic: Old names you will still hear
children.note: Trading, profit and loss account = statement of profit or loss. Balance sheet = statement of financial position. Same ideas, newer names used by IFRS.

manas.q: What are the older names for the two final accounts?

children.note: One statement shows how the business performed over the year. The other is a snapshot of what it owns and owes on the last day.
Shows income minus expenses for the year, giving profit or loss. It has two parts: the trading part (gross profit) and the expenses part (net profit).

manas.q: What does the statement of profit or loss show?

children.note: Shows, on one date, what the business owns (assets), what it owes others (liabilities) and what it owes the owner (capital). Assets = capital + liabilities.

manas.q: What does the statement of financial position show?

children.note: Money made from buying and selling goods: net sales minus cost of sales. It ignores rent, wages and other running costs.

manas.q: What is gross profit?

children.note: Opening inventory + purchases (less returns, plus carriage inwards) − closing inventory. It is the cost of the goods actually sold this year.

manas.q: How do you calculate cost of sales?

children.note: Gross profit minus the running costs (expenses) such as rent, wages and electricity. If expenses are bigger, the result is a net loss.

manas.q: What is net profit?

children.note: Opening capital + capital introduced + net profit − drawings = closing capital. A net loss is taken away instead of added.

manas.q: How do you find closing capital?

children.note: Non-current assets are kept for more than a year to run the business (van, shop fittings). Current assets turn into cash within a year (inventory, debtors, cash).

manas.q: What is the difference between non-current and current assets?

children.note: Current liabilities are due within one year (suppliers, overdraft). Non-current liabilities are due later (a bank loan repayable over three years).

manas.q: What is the difference between current and non-current liabilities?

children.note: IAS 1 Presentation of Financial Statements sets the layout for full IFRS. Small Kenyan businesses often follow IFRS for SMEs, which uses the same two statements in a simpler way.

children.topic: From trial balance to final accounts
children.note: Each trial balance item goes to one place: income and expenses to profit or loss, assets, liabilities, capital and drawings to financial position.
Mark each line P (profit or loss) or F (financial position). Each item is used once, except closing inventory, which is used twice.

manas.q: How do you sort trial balance items for the final accounts?

children.note: Start with opening inventory, add net purchases and carriage inwards, then take away closing inventory counted on the last day.
Net sales minus cost of sales gives gross profit. Take away every expense to reach net profit.
Non-current assets first, then current assets in order: inventory, receivables, bank, cash. Add for total assets.
Show the capital working (opening + profit − drawings), then non-current and current liabilities. The total must equal total assets.
It is not in the trial balance; it comes from the stock count. It reduces cost of sales and it appears as a current asset.

manas.q: Why does closing inventory appear twice in final accounts?

children.note: Income and expense accounts are closed to profit or loss at year end. Example: Dr Sales / Cr Profit or loss; Dr Profit or loss / Cr Rent. Profit is then moved to capital.
Dr Inventory (statement of financial position) / Cr Cost of sales. The asset is carried into next year as opening inventory.

manas.q: What is the journal entry for closing inventory?

children.note: Real accounts also adjust for accruals and prepayments, depreciation and bad debts. These come in the next topics; here we use the trial balance as it stands.
Wanjiku runs a small shop in Kawangware, Nairobi. Here is her trial balance at 31 December 2025, turned into both statements. All amounts in KES.
The totals agree at KES 2,850,000 on each side. Capital is KES 510,000. Closing inventory counted on 31 Dec is KES 180,000 (not in the trial balance).
Purchases 1,200,000; opening inventory 150,000; sales returns 20,000; carriage inwards 10,000; rent 240,000; wages 180,000; electricity 36,000.
Delivery costs 24,000; shop fittings 300,000; motor van 400,000; trade receivables 60,000; bank 95,000; cash 15,000; drawings 120,000. Total debits 2,850,000.
Sales 2,000,000; purchase returns 30,000; trade payables 110,000; bank loan (repay 2029) 200,000; capital 510,000. Total credits 2,850,000.
Sales 2,000,000 − returns 20,000 = net sales 1,980,000. Less cost of sales 1,150,000. Gross profit = KES 830,000.
Purchases 1,200,000 − purchase returns 30,000 + carriage inwards 10,000 = 1,180,000.
Opening inventory 150,000 + net purchases 1,180,000 = goods available 1,330,000. Less closing inventory 180,000 = cost of sales 1,150,000.
Rent 240,000 + wages 180,000 + electricity 36,000 + delivery costs 24,000 = expenses 480,000. Net profit = 830,000 − 480,000 = KES 350,000.
Non-current: van 400,000 + fittings 300,000 = 700,000. Current: inventory 180,000 + receivables 60,000 + bank 95,000 + cash 15,000 = 350,000. Total assets KES 1,050,000.
Capital 510,000 + profit 350,000 − drawings 120,000 = 740,000. Add bank loan 200,000 and payables 110,000. Total KES 1,050,000.
Total assets 1,050,000 = capital and liabilities 1,050,000. If your two totals differ, check that every trial balance line was used exactly once.
Gross margin = 830,000 ÷ 1,980,000 ≈ 41.9%. Net margin = 350,000 ÷ 1,980,000 ≈ 17.7%. Ratios get a full topic later.

children.topic: Owner took goods for home use
children.note: If Wanjiku takes stock costing KES 5,000 for her family: Dr Drawings 5,000 / Cr Purchases 5,000. It is not a sale and not an expense.

manas.q: What is the entry when the owner takes goods for personal use?

children.note: Most lost marks come from putting an item in the wrong statement or using it twice.
Wrong. Drawings reduce capital on the statement of financial position. They never reduce profit.

manas.q: Where do drawings go in the final accounts?

children.note: Carriage inwards (bringing goods in) is added to cost of sales. Carriage outwards (delivering to customers) is an expense below gross profit.

manas.q: Where do carriage inwards and carriage outwards go?

children.note: Sales returns are taken off sales. Purchase returns are taken off purchases. Do not show them as income or expenses.

children.topic: Using opening inventory as an asset
children.note: Only closing inventory is an asset at the year end. Opening inventory goes only into cost of sales.

children.topic: Buying an asset is not an expense
children.note: A van or fittings bought for the business is a non-current asset, not a cost in profit or loss (capital vs revenue spending).

manas.q: Is the purchase of a motor van an expense?

children.note: A loan repayable after 12 months is non-current. Any part due within the next year is current. Read the dates in the question.
Write the business name, the statement name and "for the year ended" or "as at". Examiners give marks for format.

manas.q: What date wording goes on each statement?

children.note: Try each one on paper first, then open the answer steps.

children.topic: Q1: Find cost of sales and gross profit
children.note: Opening inventory 40,000; purchases 300,000; closing inventory 50,000; sales 450,000. Find cost of sales and gross profit.
A matatu owner starts the year with capital of KES 600,000, makes a net profit of 150,000 and draws 90,000. Find closing capital.

children.topic: Q3: Closing capital after a loss
children.note: Opening capital 300,000; net loss 40,000; drawings 30,000. Find closing capital.
300,000 − 40,000 − 30,000 = KES 230,000. A loss and drawings both reduce capital.
Where do these go: carriage outwards, a delivery van, an overdraft, closing inventory?
Carriage outwards: expense in profit or loss. Van: non-current asset. Overdraft: current liability. Closing inventory: cost of sales and current asset.
